H.quirks: The most abundant element in the universe, yet free hydrogen is rare on Earth because it escapes to space.

He.quirks: Found in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, 27 years before it was found on Earth. Liquid helium creeps up and over the walls of its container.

Li.quirks: 7 Up originally contained lithium citrate as a mood lifter until 1948.

Be.quirks: Beryllium salts taste sweet, which is how chemists once tested them, a dangerous habit. Emerald and aquamarine are beryllium minerals.

B.quirks: Boron gives a green flame. Pyrex owes its heat resistance to boron oxide.

C.quirks: Carbon-14 lets archaeologists date anything that once lived. Graphite and diamond are the same element.

N.quirks: Fritz Haber won a Nobel Prize for fixing nitrogen and also led Germany's poison gas programme.

O.quirks: Liquid oxygen is pale blue and sticks to a magnet.

F.quirks: Several chemists were poisoned trying to isolate fluorine before Henri Moissan succeeded in 1886.

Ne.quirks: 'Neon' signs in colours other than red use other gases or coloured glass.

Na.quirks: Sodium metal is soft enough to cut with a knife and must be kept under oil.

Mg.quirks: Magnesium flares burn brighter than the sun and were used in early flash photography.

Al.quirks: Aluminium was once more valuable than gold; Napoleon III served honoured guests on aluminium plates.

Si.quirks: Silicon Valley is named after silicon chips, not silicone.

P.quirks: Discovered in 1669 by an alchemist boiling down urine in search of gold.

S.quirks: Brimstone in the Bible is sulfur. Sulfur crystals crack in the warmth of your hand.

Cl.quirks: Chlorine gas was the first chemical weapon used at scale, at Ypres in 1915.

Ar.quirks: Its name means 'lazy' in Greek. Potassium–argon dating measures the age of volcanic rocks.

K.quirks: Bananas are slightly radioactive because of potassium-40.

Ca.quirks: The White Cliffs of Dover and the Antrim chalk are the skeletons of tiny sea creatures.

Sc.quirks: Mendeleev predicted it as 'eka-boron' before it was found.

Ti.quirks: Titanium burns in pure nitrogen. Self-cleaning glass uses a titanium dioxide film that breaks down dirt in sunlight.

V.quirks: Named after a Norse goddess for its many colourful compounds. Sea squirts concentrate vanadium in their blood.

Cr.quirks: Chromium gives rubies their red and emeralds their green.

Mn.quirks: Cave paintings at Lascaux used manganese oxide for black.

Fe.quirks: The Earth's core is mostly iron, which creates the magnetic field that protects us from solar wind.

Co.quirks: Named after 'kobolds', goblins miners blamed for ores that gave off toxic fumes.

Ni.quirks: Named from 'Kupfernickel', devil's copper, because the ore looked like copper but yielded none.

Cu.quirks: The Statue of Liberty is copper turned green.

Zn.quirks: Zinc is in brass, and brass instruments are mostly copper and zinc.

Ga.quirks: Melts in your hand (about 30 °C). It is used in 'disappearing spoon' tricks because a gallium spoon melts in hot tea.

Ge.quirks: The first transistor, in 1947, was made of germanium.

As.quirks: Napoleon's hair contained arsenic, possibly from green wallpaper.

Se.quirks: Garlic breath can come from selenium: workers exposed to it smell of garlic.

Br.quirks: One of only two elements liquid at room temperature; the other is mercury.

Sr.quirks: Named after the Scottish village of Strontian, where it was first found.

Zr.quirks: Cubic zirconia is a cheap diamond imitation that is actually harder to scratch than glass.

Nb.quirks: Named after Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, because it is so like tantalum.

Mo.quirks: Its name comes from Greek for 'lead', because it was long mistaken for lead.

Rh.quirks: Thieves target catalytic converters for the rhodium, palladium and platinum inside.

Pd.quirks: Named after the asteroid Pallas, discovered the year before.

Ag.quirks: Silver iodide has been used in cloud seeding to try to make rain or snow.

Cd.quirks: Named from 'cadmia', an old word for zinc ore.

Sn.quirks: Tin 'cries' with a creaking sound when bent. In cold, it can crumble to powder ('tin pest').

Sb.quirks: Ancient Egyptians used antimony sulfide as kohl eyeliner. 'Everlasting pills' of antimony were swallowed as a laxative, recovered and reused.

I.quirks: First found in seaweed ash, used for making gunpowder in Napoleonic France. Solid iodine turns straight to violet vapour.

Cs.quirks: The most reactive metal you can hold in a sealed glass ampoule; it melts at 28 °C.

Ba.quirks: Bologna stone, a barium mineral, was the first known glow-in-the-dark material, in 1603.

Nd.quirks: Neodymium glass is used in welding goggles and makes things look different under different light.

Ta.quirks: Named after Tantalus because it cannot absorb acid, as Tantalus could never drink.

W.quirks: Its symbol W comes from 'wolfram', from the German for 'wolf's froth'. Tungsten is as dense as gold, so it is used to fake gold bars.

Ir.quirks: The most corrosion-resistant metal. The 1980 iridium discovery changed how we think about mass extinctions.

Pt.quirks: Spanish explorers once threw platinum away as worthless 'little silver'. The kilogram was defined by a platinum-iridium cylinder until 2019.

Au.quirks: All the gold ever mined would fit in a cube about 22 metres a side. Gold leaf can be beaten thin enough to let green light through.

Hg.quirks: 'Mad as a hatter' comes from hat-makers poisoned by mercury used on felt.

Pb.quirks: The Romans sweetened wine with lead acetate, 'sugar of lead'.

Bi.quirks: Grows staircase-shaped crystals with rainbow colours. It is very slightly radioactive, with a half-life a billion times the age of the universe.

Rn.quirks: Radon spas in Europe still advertise radon baths as therapy.

U.quirks: Uranium glass glows green under UV light, and old Fiestaware plates are radioactive.
